content.overview: Effective sanitation is a controlled sequence: remove debris, clean, apply the approved disinfection process as directed, verify completion and record exceptions.

vocabulary.definition: Physical removal of soil, debris, organic matter and residues from a surface or item.
Use of an appropriate process to reduce or inactivate specified microorganisms on a cleaned surface or item.
The period a disinfectant must remain in contact with a surface as directed by its label or procedure.

sections.title: Clean before disinfecting
sections.body: UMass greenhouse guidance emphasizes removal of debris and organic matter before disinfection because residues can protect organisms or reduce the effectiveness of some disinfectants.

sections.title: Follow the approved product and process
sections.body: Disinfectants differ in labeled uses, concentrations, contact times, hazards and material compatibility. Technicians follow the current label and SOP, verify the required conditions and document incomplete or failed sanitation rather than inventing concentrations or mixing products.

workedExamples: Root debris is physically removed from a bench before the approved disinfectant is applied.
A sanitizer label does not match the SOP, so the technician stops and verifies the correct product instead of substituting.
commonMistakes: Applying disinfectant over heavy organic debris and assuming the surface is sanitized.
Using a stronger concentration because it seems safer.
content.practicalApplication: Sequence a sanitation work order from debris removal through cleaning, label/SOP verification, disinfection, final check and documentation.
content.summary: Sanitation is not cosmetic. Clean first, use the approved product as directed, verify completion and document any exception.

blocks.title: Cleaning and disinfection are different operations
blocks.body: Cleaning physically removes soil, media, plant debris, organic matter, and residues. Disinfection is a separate approved process used on appropriate cleaned surfaces or equipment. Organic debris can interfere with contact or reduce the effectiveness of some disinfectants, so a dirty surface is not made controlled merely by spraying over it.

blocks.alt: Nine-step sanitation workflow showing secure or remove material, remove debris and gross soil, physically clean, verify the approved product and preparation, apply as directed, maintain required contact conditions, complete the required finish step, inspect the result, and document completion or exceptions.
blocks.caption: A generic learning sequence; the exact product preparation, application, contact conditions, rinse/dry requirements, and compatibility rules come from the current label and facility SOP.

items.title: Prepare the work area
items.body: Secure or remove plant/material as required by the procedure and prevent uncontrolled movement during the task.

items.title: Remove gross contamination
items.body: Take away roots, media, plant debris, and other material that would block effective cleaning or product contact.

items.title: Clean physically
items.body: Use the defined cleaning method for the surface or equipment before the disinfection step.

items.title: Verify the product and preparation
items.body: Confirm the exact approved product, label, dilution/preparation, compatibility, and PPE requirements; do not substitute by brand familiarity.

items.title: Apply and maintain required conditions
items.body: Use the product as directed and maintain the specified contact or wet conditions where applicable.

items.title: Finish, inspect, and document
items.body: Complete any required rinse/dry/finish step, inspect the result, and record completion or exceptions honestly.

blocks.title: Do not strengthen, combine, or substitute by intuition
blocks.body: Disinfectants and cleaners differ in labeled use, concentration, contact conditions, hazards, and material compatibility. A Technician I worker follows the current label and SOP instead of making a stronger mix, combining unknown products, or substituting a similar-looking product.

blocks.title: Controlled sanitation versus a cosmetic shortcut

left.label: Controlled process
left.body: Root debris is removed, the surface is cleaned, the approved product and preparation are verified, the disinfection step is completed as directed, and the result is inspected and documented.

right.label: Shortcut
right.body: Disinfectant is sprayed over heavy organic debris and the area is marked complete because the surface looks wet and smells clean.

blocks.title: Same brand, different product
blocks.setting: The SOP names one sanitizer, but the container on the cart is from the same manufacturer with a different active ingredient and different label directions.
blocks.prompt: What is the best first response?
options: Use it because the brand is the same
Double-check the color and use it if it looks similar
Stop and verify the approved product and current instructions before proceeding
Use a stronger mix so the substitution is more effective
blocks.answer: Stop and verify the approved product and current instructions before proceeding.
blocks.feedback: Brand similarity is not evidence that products are interchangeable. The controlling label and facility procedure determine the approved use and preparation.

blocks.title: Sequence and error hunt
blocks.instructions: Arrange a supplied sanitation task into the correct sequence, then remove unsupported actions and explain the main consequence of each error.
prompts: Place valid steps from material control through final documentation in order.
Flag any action that applies disinfectant over heavy debris.
Flag any action that changes concentration without the controlling instruction.
Flag any step that substitutes or combines products without authorization.
Identify whether each error primarily threatens efficacy, worker safety, material compatibility, traceability, or more than one of these.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Sanitation is a verifiable process, not an appearance. Clean first, use the exact approved process, meet the required conditions, inspect the result, and document exceptions rather than hiding incomplete work.
